html:
Semantic memory, as used here, is the brain’s long-horizon statistical model of the world: a store of decontextualized, recombinable knowledge that supports rapid generalization across tasks and modalities. As said by Binder et al: "semantic memory is one of our most defining human traits, encompassing all the declarative knowledge we acquire about the world. A short list of examples includes the names and physical attributes of all objects, the origin and history of objects, the names and attributes of actions, all abstract concepts and their names, knowledge of how people behave and why, opinions and beliefs, knowledge of historical events, knowledge of causes and effects, associations between concepts, categories and their bases, and on and on ... humans use conceptual knowledge for much more than merely interacting with objects. All of human culture, including science, literature, social institutions, religion, and art, is constructed from conceptual knowledge. We do not reason, plan the future or remember the past without conceptual content - all of these activities depend on activation of concepts stored in semantic memory." 1.

Contemporary accounts converge on a two-system view-rich, transmodal representations plus control processes that shape retrieval to current goals-while also emphasizing that these functions are distributed, graded, and embedded in the cortex’s macroscale organization 2. Natural-speech fMRI shows semantic information tiling large swaths of temporal, parietal, and prefrontal cortex, overlapping substantially with the transmodal apex of the principal connectivity gradient (the default-mode end) 3, 4, rather than any single "language" area 5. A 2026 model study compares learned concept layers with human brain representations (Figure) 12.

Evidence from neuropsychology, stimulation, and ATL-optimized fMRI supports a "hub-and-spoke" organization in which modality-biased spokes (visual, motor, affective, linguistic) project to a graded semantic hub centered in ventral/anterior temporal cortex; the hub’s subregions show smooth shifts in bias rather than sharp boundaries 6. This view accommodates both "semantic tiles" observed with voxelwise encoding models 5 and transmodal integration demanded by concept combination and generalization, and it explains classic semantic dementia phenotypes 7. Debates continue over additional hubs (e.g., angular gyrus), but current syntheses place AG as a heteromodal integrator/buffer interfacing DMN with language-perceptual systems rather than a sole amodal store 8.

This cortical schema rides on long-range white-matter "highways." Ventral pathways-the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (occipito-temporal), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (occipito-frontal), and uncinate fasciculus (temporal-orbitofrontal)-link perceptual areas with anterior temporal and prefrontal hubs; dorsal streams (superior longitudinal/arcuate) and the cingulum bind semantic regions with control and mnemonic networks. Lesion mapping, intraoperative stimulation, and diffusion imaging converge on these tracts as the structural backbone enabling fast access to distributed conceptual content during comprehension and production 9, 10, 11.

Functionally, the control side of the system is left-leaning and includes inferior frontal gyrus and posterior middle temporal cortex, among others; meta-analyses and surface-based state-space work show that network configuration shifts with association strength and task demands, flexing along the principal gradient from sensory-coupled to transmodal states. During retrieval, humans exhibit "semantic foraging"-cluster-and-switch search through conceptual space-supported by frontoparietal control and DMN-adjacent buffers. Over learning timescales, hippocampal-neocortical complementarities and schema effects help explain how episodic traces are distilled ("semanticized") into durable cortical structure, with schema-consistent knowledge integrating more rapidly.
